fields.Page Content:
Backchecking in Floorball is a defensive transition action that happens the moment your team loses possession and the opponent starts moving forward. Unlike forechecking, which applies pressure high up the court, backchecking focuses on sprinting back, reorganizing, and preventing the opponent from gaining an advantage in the counterattack.

The purpose of backchecking is to delay, disrupt, or completely neutralize the opponent’s transition before they reach a dangerous offensive position. Effective backchecking includes:

  • Closing the middle first and protecting the slot
  • Picking up the nearest free attacker
  • Forcing the opponent to slow down or play wide
  • Tracking runners all the way into the defensive zone

Backchecking is a core part of a team’s defensive transition principles. The goal is to regain defensive structure as quickly as possible so the opponent cannot create odd-man situations such as 2 vs 1 or 3 vs 2 in front of your goal.
fields.Headline: What is Backchecking?
fields.Name: Backchecking

fields.Page Content:
Boxplay in Floorball is the defensive structure your team uses when you are short-handed (playing with fewer players due to a penalty). The goal is to protect the most dangerous areas first, reduce high-quality shots, and force the attacking team to play around the outside.

The core idea is simple: you do not chase the ball, you manage space. A good boxplay keeps the slot closed, communicates on switches, and times pressure so the opponent cannot create easy one-timers or backdoor tap-ins.

Key characteristics of an effective boxplay:

  • Protect the low slot and keep sticks in passing lanes
  • Shift as a unit toward the ball side while staying compact
  • Apply pressure on bad touches or predictable passes (not constantly)
  • Clear rebounds and win loose balls to get a chance to clear
  • Look for intercepts and quick clears to change momentum

In coaching terms, boxplay is about discipline and repetition. Teams that defend penalties well often survive long stretches without giving up “free” chances, and they turn penalty kills into confidence and energy. A clean boxplay also helps your goalie by keeping shots visible and predictable.
fields.Headline: What is Boxplay?
fields.Name: Boxplay

fields.Page Content:
Counter-Press in Floorball is the immediate pressure your team applies right after losing possession to prevent the opponent from starting a clean counterattack. It happens in the first seconds after a turnover and is one of the fastest ways to control transitions.

Instead of sprinting back instantly, the nearest players “lock” the ball carrier, cut off simple outlets, and try to force a mistake or win the ball back. The goal is not reckless chasing, it is to buy time and stop the opponent from accelerating through the middle.

Common elements of a good counter-press:

  • Pressure the ball with the closest player in a controlled angle
  • Close the middle first and force play toward the boards
  • Mark the most dangerous passing options (especially the slot runner)
  • Communicate who presses and who covers behind
  • If the ball is not won quickly, transition into backchecking structure

Counter-pressing is a coaching tool to reduce odd-man rushes like 2 vs 1 or 3 vs 2. Done well, it creates extra possessions high up the court and keeps your team on the front foot. Done poorly, it opens space behind the press, so timing and roles matter.
fields.Headline: What is Counter-Press?
fields.Name: Counter-Press

fields.Page Content:
Defense Zone in Floorball is the part of the court closest to your own goal where your team’s main job is to protect the slot, limit dangerous shots, and regain possession safely. Teams often talk about zones to simplify tactics: where you defend, where you press, and where you want to force the opponent.

In the defense zone, the priority is not to win the ball at any cost. It is to stay organized, protect high-danger space, and reduce chaos in front of your goalie. Good teams defend “inside-out”: they secure the middle first and give up low-value shots from wide angles.

Key principles in the defense zone:

  • Keep the slot crowded with sticks on the floor and bodies in lanes
  • Track runners and eliminate backdoor options at the long post
  • Communicate switches and maintain compact distances between players
  • Win rebounds and loose balls, then make a simple first pass out
  • Avoid unnecessary fouls and risky dribbles in the middle

For coaches, the defense zone is where structure shows. If your team can stay calm here, you concede fewer goals and you start more transitions after winning the ball. If structure breaks, you give the opponent second chances through rebounds and quick passes into the slot.
fields.Headline: What is Defense Zone?
fields.Name: Defense Zone

fields.Page Content:
East-West in Floorball describes ball movement that goes side-to-side across the court, rather than forward toward the goal. East-west passing is used to shift the defense, change the angle of attack, and create better lanes for shots, one-timers, or penetration.

The tactical purpose is to move defenders. When the ball travels laterally, defenders must rotate, adjust sticks, and decide whether to step or stay compact. If the ball moves faster than the defense, gaps appear in the slot, at the long post, or in the pocket between lines.

Key characteristics of effective east-west play:

  • Pass with tempo so the defense cannot reset
  • Use width to pull defenders out of the middle
  • Combine with quick “north-south” actions after the shift (drive or shot)
  • Create one-timer lanes by changing the ball side
  • Avoid slow, predictable sideways passes that invite pressure

East-west is not automatically good. Sideways passes that are too soft or too obvious can lead to interceptions and counters. The best teams use east-west to prepare a decisive action: a direct pass into the slot, a one-timer, or a switch that opens the weak-side runner.
fields.Headline: What is East-West?
fields.Name: East-West

fields.Page Content:
Forechecking in Floorball is a defensive strategy where your team applies pressure high up the court while the opponent is trying to build up play, typically in their defensive zone or as they enter the neutral zone. The goal is to disrupt clean exits, force predictable decisions, and win possession in a favorable area.

Forechecking is not random chasing. It is coordinated pressure that closes time and space for the opponent’s defenders and center while taking away the most valuable passing lanes. Good forechecking sets the opponent into uncomfortable touches and “traps” that lead to turnovers.

Key characteristics of an effective forecheck:

  • Pressure the ball carrier with the right angle to force play wide or into a trap
  • Close nearby options so the opponent cannot play out easily
  • Keep compact team distances so the press cannot be played through
  • Use clear structures (for example 2–1–2 or 2–2–1) with defined roles
  • If the opponent breaks the forecheck, recover quickly into defensive shape

For coaches, forechecking defines the team’s defensive identity and tempo. A strong forecheck creates more possessions near the opponent’s goal and limits their controlled attacks. The tradeoff is risk: if timing and spacing are off, the opponent can bypass pressure and create transition chances.
fields.Headline: What is Forechecking?
fields.Name: Forechecking

fields.Page Content:
Inside in Floorball usually refers to the central corridor of the court, especially the space in and around the slot. “Inside defending” means prioritizing the middle, denying passes into dangerous areas, and forcing the opponent to play toward the boards.

The tactical purpose is to reduce high-quality chances. Most goals are scored from central positions because of better angles, shorter distance, screens, and rebounds. If your team controls the inside, the opponent is often limited to low-percentage shots from wide or from the corners.

Key principles when defending inside:

  • Stay between the attacker and the goal, closing the middle first
  • Keep your stick in the passing lane into the slot or long post
  • Angle pressure so the ball carrier is guided outside
  • Communicate switches so runners do not get inside positioning
  • Be patient: do not overcommit and open the inside lane

For coaches, “inside first” is a simple rule that improves team defending immediately. It creates consistent priorities across defensive systems. When players understand inside space, they read transitions faster and protect the goal even under pressure.
fields.Headline: What is Inside?
fields.Name: Inside

fields.Page Content:
Long Post in Floorball is the far side of the goal relative to where the ball is. If the ball is on the right side, the long post is on the left side of the goal (and vice versa). It is a key reference point because many goals come from passes or rebounds that travel across the goal mouth to that far side.

Offensively, the long post is where “backdoor” chances happen. Defensively, it is where teams get punished when they ball-watch and lose their weak-side responsibility.

Key long-post concepts:

  • The long-post attacker is often the most dangerous off-ball player
  • Quick passes across the slot create tap-ins at the far post
  • On rebounds, the long post is a common second-chance scoring area
  • Defenders must scan and shoulder-check to avoid losing their mark
  • Goalies often have to move laterally, making timing critical

Coaching use is straightforward: teach players to identify the long post in every situation. Attackers learn when to arrive and when to stay ready for a one-touch finish. Defenders learn to protect inside position and track the weak-side runner all the way into the defensive zone.
fields.Headline: What is Long Post?
fields.Name: Long Post

fields.Page Content:
Neutral Zone in Floorball is the middle area of the court between the two teams’ defensive zones. It is where many transitions happen: teams try to break pressure, enter the offensive zone, or stop the opponent’s zone entry.

The tactical purpose of neutral-zone play is to control the “connection” between defense and attack. If you manage this space well, you enter with speed and structure. If you lose it, you give the opponent counters with numbers and space.

Key characteristics of strong neutral-zone play:

  • Provide passing options at different depths (short and long)
  • Use width to escape pressure, then attack the inside lane
  • Support the ball so turnovers do not become odd-man rushes
  • Defensively, close the middle and force the ball wide
  • Time pressure so you can win the ball without breaking structure

For coaches, the neutral zone is a great place to define team principles: how you want to press, where you want to funnel, and what a “good” zone entry looks like. Many games are decided here because clean neutral-zone decisions reduce turnovers and create better attacking possessions.
fields.Headline: What is Neutral Zone?
fields.Name: Neutral Zone

fields.Page Content:
Offensive Zone in Floorball is the part of the court closest to the opponent’s goal where your team tries to create scoring chances. It is where spacing, timing, and decision making matter most because the defense is compact and mistakes are punished with quick counters.

The tactical purpose of offensive-zone play is to generate high-quality chances: passes into the slot, one-timers, screens, rebounds, and backdoor finishes at the long post. Good teams keep possession long enough to move defenders and then attack the inside at the right moment.

Key offensive-zone principles:

  • Create width and depth so passing lanes open into the slot
  • Move the ball with tempo (east-west) to shift defenders
  • Put players in scoring roles: shooter, screener, rebounder, playmaker
  • Be ready for loss of possession with immediate counter-press/backcheck
  • Avoid forced plays through the middle when the defense is set

From a coaching perspective, the offensive zone is where a team’s identity shows: structured patterns versus more free play, how you use the corners, and how you attack the slot. The best offenses do not just shoot, they create conditions that make the goalie’s job difficult.
fields.Headline: What is Offensive Zone?
fields.Name: Offensive Zone

fields.Page Content:
One Timer in Floorball is a shot taken directly off a pass, without stopping or controlling the ball first. The shooter receives the ball and shoots in one motion, which reduces the goalie’s reaction time and makes the defense’s positioning less effective.

The tactical purpose of a one-timer is speed. Because the ball changes angle quickly, the goalie must move laterally and often cannot set their feet. One-timers are especially dangerous from the high slot or on the weak side after an east-west pass.

Key characteristics of a good one-timer:

  • Arrive early and be set with your body facing the target area
  • Keep your stick on the floor and prepare the shooting motion before the pass
  • Call for the ball and time your movement into space
  • Shoot quickly and accurately, often low for rebounds or far side for goals
  • If the pass is not perfect, adjust with a controlled touch rather than forcing

For coaches, one-timers are both a technical and tactical skill. They require repetition, but also the right team spacing and timing to open the lane. A team that threatens with one-timers forces defenders to collapse, which can open space for passes into the slot or to the long post.
fields.Headline: What is One Timer?
fields.Name: One Timer

fields.Page Content:
Playbook in Floorball is the collection of your team’s agreed solutions for common situations: how you build up, how you enter zones, how you defend, and what you do in special teams. A playbook does not mean every action is scripted. It provides shared language and clear roles so players make the same decisions under pressure.

The tactical purpose of a playbook is consistency. When everyone recognizes the situation and the cues, the team moves faster and with less hesitation. That matters most in transitions, in the offensive zone, and in moments like powerplay and boxplay where structure creates advantages.

Typical elements you find in a Floorball playbook:

  • Principles (inside defending, transition rules, pressing triggers)
  • Systems (forecheck shapes, defensive formations, neutral-zone behaviors)
  • Set plays (face-off routines, zone entry patterns, end-game scenarios)
  • Special teams (powerplay and boxplay structures, clearing rules)
  • Communication terms so players can coordinate quickly during a shift

For coaches, a playbook is a teaching tool and a reference point. It helps you build progressions: start with simple principles, then add options and adjustments. For players, it reduces uncertainty and improves chemistry, because teammates can anticipate each other’s movement instead of reacting late.
fields.Headline: What is Playbook?
fields.Name: Playbook

fields.Page Content:
In a 2-1-2 defense system in Floorball, open space appears on both sides of the center.

This space is behind the forwards but too high for the defenders to step up without leaving their positions.

Because the space exists on both sides, the center cannot cover everything at the same time.

We draw in yellow the pockets in a 2-1-2 defensive formation

![](assets/2f51e0bb88128024b8a7cc23e19bb9ff/0001-image.png)
fields.Headline: What is the pocket?
fields.Name: Pocket

fields.Page Content:
Powerplay in Floorball is the attacking situation when your team has a player advantage because the opponent has a penalty. The goal is to use the extra player to create high-quality chances, typically through ball movement that opens the slot and creates one-timers or backdoor finishes.

The tactical purpose is to force defenders to cover more space than they can. With patience and tempo, you can shift the boxplay, open lanes, and get the goalie moving. A good powerplay is not only about shooting more, it is about shooting better.

Common powerplay principles:

  • Keep possession and move the ball quickly (east-west) to shift the defense
  • Create a clear structure: point options, half-wall options, slot presence
  • Threaten with a one-timer to force defenders to collapse
  • Use screens and rebounds in front of the goalie
  • Be ready for counters if a pass is intercepted or a shot is blocked

For coaches, powerplay is a repeatable “special teams” phase. The best powerplays score because they create predictable reads for the attackers while still forcing unpredictable problems for the defenders.
fields.Headline: What is Powerplay?
fields.Name: Powerplay

fields.Page Content:
Pressing in Floorball is an aggressive defensive approach where your team actively applies pressure to the ball and nearby passing options to win possession or force mistakes. Pressing is about coordinated team movement, not one player chasing the ball alone.

The tactical purpose is to disrupt the opponent’s build-up and prevent controlled attacks. By closing time and space, you force rushed passes, poor touches, or predictable clears. Pressing can happen high in the offensive zone, in the neutral zone, or situationally after certain triggers.

Key characteristics of effective pressing:

  • Clear roles: who pressures the ball, who covers lanes, who supports behind
  • Compact distances so the press does not get played through easily
  • Angled pressure to guide the opponent toward the boards or into traps
  • Triggers such as a bad touch, backhand control, or slow pass
  • If the press fails, immediate recovery into defensive structure

Pressing is a coaching choice with risk and reward. Done well, it creates turnovers close to the opponent’s goal and keeps the game in your preferred tempo. Done poorly, it opens space behind the press and leads to odd-man situations, so team synchronization and communication are critical.
fields.Headline: What is Pressing?
fields.Name: Pressing

fields.Page Content:
The player standing in front of the goalie to block/ reduce their view while a teammate shoots.

It is a tactical action where the player positions themselves directly in front of the opponent’s goalie.

Purpose and Effect

  • Block the goalie’s view: The screener takes away the goalie’s clear line of sight to the ball and the shooter.
  • Reduce reaction time: If the goalie cannot see the ball early, they react later — which greatly increases the chance of scoring, especially on shots from distance.
  • Ready for rebounds: The screener is close to the goal to score from rebounds if the goalie cannot control the save.

How to Screen?

  • Positioning: The player stands or moves into the slot. Close enough to block the goalie’s view while still being playable for passes or rebounds but not blocking the actual shot
  • Body position: The player stays low and balanced to avoid being pushed away by defenders.
  • Stick control: The stick is kept on the floor to receive passes, redirect shots, or score quick tap-ins, while the body blocks the goalie’s vision.
  • Movement: A good screener adjusts their position with the ball movement to stay in the goalie’s line of sight.

What to avoid?

  • Allowed vs. not allowed: Screening with your body is allowed. Actively pushing, hitting, or blocking the goalie is not allowed and can lead to a penalty for goalie interference.
  • Goal area awareness: The player must respect the goal area rules. Illegal positioning too close to the goalie can result in a disallowed goal.

Why Screening Matters

Screening is a key element in modern Floorball. Goalies are fast and well-positioned, and scoring clean goals without blocking their view is difficult. Good screening creates chaos, space, and scoring chances.
fields.Headline: What is a screen in Floorball?
fields.Name: Screen

fields.Page Content:
Slot in Floorball is the central scoring area in front of the goal. It is where the most dangerous shots and goals happen because players are close to the net, angles are better, and rebounds and screens create chaos for the goalie and defenders.

The tactical purpose of the slot is simple: offensively you want to access it, defensively you want to protect it. Many team principles (inside defending, boxplay, weak-side awareness) are basically different ways of managing slot space.

Key characteristics of slot play:

  • High danger because of short distance and direct shooting angles
  • Frequent rebounds, loose balls, and second-chance finishes
  • Screens reduce the goalie’s vision and reaction time
  • Slot passes force defenders to collapse and create one-timers elsewhere
  • Physical battles for inside position, especially in front of the goalie

Coaches often divide the slot into the low slot (right in front of the goal) and the high slot (a bit higher with more space). The low slot produces tap-ins, rebounds, and screens. The high slot produces one-timers, quick releases, and playmaking. If your team can consistently win slot positioning, you will score more and concede less, regardless of system.
fields.Headline: What is Slot?
fields.Name: Slot

fields.Page Content:
Transition in Floorball is the phase where play changes from defense to offense or from offense to defense. Transitions happen after turnovers, rebounds, blocked shots, or when possession changes during open play.

The tactical purpose is to take advantage of moments when the opponent is not organized. In offensive transition, you want speed, support, and clear decisions to create a quick chance. In defensive transition, you want immediate recovery: counter-press, backchecking, and protecting the inside so you do not concede an easy goal.

Key characteristics of strong transition play:

  • Quick scanning and first decision (pass, carry, or reset)
  • Sprinting support to create passing options and numbers
  • Protecting the middle lane first when defending transition
  • Clear communication: who presses, who covers, who picks up runners
  • If no advantage exists, slow down and build structured possession

For coaches, transitions are where principles outperform set plays. A team with clear transition rules will look faster even without faster players, because everyone reacts the same way. Many decisive goals in Floorball come from transition moments, so training these situations consistently is a high-value investment.
fields.Headline: What is Transition?
fields.Name: Transition

fields.Page Content:
Weak-Side in Floorball is the side of the court away from the ball. When the ball is on the right, the left side is the weak side (and vice versa). It matters because goals often come from weak-side movement: late arrivals into the slot, long-post tap-ins, and one-timers after an east-west switch.

The tactical purpose of weak-side play is to create or deny space. Offensively, you attack the weak side because defenders tend to collapse toward the ball. Defensively, you must stay aware of the weak-side runner and not get pulled entirely toward the ball carrier.

Key weak-side concepts:

  • Weak-side attackers time their runs for backdoor chances at the long post
  • Weak-side defenders must scan and keep inside position, not just ball-watch
  • A fast switch of play can create immediate one-timer opportunities
  • Good teams keep weak-side spacing to stretch the defense horizontally
  • In transitions, weak-side responsibility is often the first thing to break

For coaches, “weak-side awareness” is a repeatable habit: shoulder-checking, communication, and assigning responsibility. Teams that manage the weak side well give up fewer easy goals and create more high-quality chances with simple switches of play.
fields.Headline: What is Weak-Side?
fields.Name: Weak-Side

fields.Page Content:
Zone Entry in Floorball is the moment your team moves the ball from the neutral zone into the opponent’s offensive zone with the goal of starting a controlled attack. A clean zone entry allows you to keep possession, establish spacing, and create scoring chances instead of dumping the ball away and defending a counter.

The tactical purpose is to break the opponent’s pressure and enter with advantage. The defense tries to deny entries by closing the middle, steering you wide, or forcing risky passes. Your job is to enter with structure and support so the ball carrier has options.

Key characteristics of effective zone entries:

  • Support near the ball (short option) and a deeper option to stretch defenders
  • Use width to escape pressure, then attack inside at the right time
  • Timing: move without the ball so the carrier has clear passing lanes
  • If the entry is not clean, reset and keep possession rather than forcing
  • Be ready for defensive transition if the entry fails (counter-press/backcheck)

For coaches, zone entry is a repeatable phase with clear teaching points. When a team improves entries, they spend more time in the offensive zone and create better chances. When entries are rushed, turnovers happen in bad positions and the opponent gets free transition attacks.
fields.Headline: What is Zone Entry?
fields.Name: Zone Entry
